column1: Why does mallet hardness affect timbre on a marimba/vibraphone, and what should it NOT be used to control?
column2: A hard mallet injects energy into high partials outside the tuned region, causing clang/noise; a soft mallet concentrates energy in the fundamental and first overtone where the bar is tuned. Mallet hardness should not be used to control loudness — stroke height controls volume.

column1: What does the undercut arch on a marimba/xylophone bar do acoustically?
column2: It pulls the bar's first two overtones into near-harmonic alignment with the fundamental (roughly an octave and a twelfth above it), making the struck bar sound 'in tune' rather than clangy.

column1: On vibraphone, what physical mechanism produces the tremolo effect, and what is it NOT (i.e. how should you treat it)?
column2: A motor-driven fan rotates inside the resonator tube mouths, periodically blocking and opening them. It is not decorative — it's a real-time timbral control (alongside mallet choice and stroke) and should be adjusted mid-performance like a knob.

column1: How does contact time between mallet/stick and the struck surface act as a built-in EQ?
column2: Longer contact (soft mallet, relaxed pressure) acts like a low-pass filter, exciting mostly low partials; shorter contact (hard mallet/stick, fast bounce-off) passes more high-frequency energy into the surface.

column1: Why do center strikes vs. edge strikes on a drumhead produce different tones, not different pitches?
column2: Fundamental pitch is set by head tension, not strike location. Center strikes drive the head's main vibrating mode, exciting the fundamental for a full, round tone; edge strikes suppress the fundamental and excite higher, faster-decaying partials for a thinner, 'ticky' sound.

column1: Explain the mechanical basis of the Moeller technique and double-stroke roll in one principle.
column2: Rebound is free energy: after impact, the head's elastic restoring force shoots the stick back up. Relaxing grip pressure at the moment of impact lets the stick rise almost on its own, rather than fighting the rebound with muscle.

column1: Why is the wrist described as a 'speed multiplier' in stick technique, and what should it NOT be used for?
column2: The arm-wrist-stick chain is a compound lever with the wrist at the far end, so small wrist rotations produce large stick-tip velocity — ideal for fast, quiet playing. Big arm swings should be reserved for volume and accents, not speed.

column1: What is the standard matched-grip fulcrum position and pressure checkpoint on a drumstick?
column2: The stick rests in the pinch between the thumb and first knuckle of the index finger, about 1/3 of the way up from the butt end (the natural balance point). Pinch only enough that the other fingers can still slightly wiggle the stick's tip — overgripping is a fault.

column1: Why do circular drumheads produce 'pitched noise' instead of a clear musical note like a string?
column2: Strings vibrate in one dimension with overtones at clean integer multiples of the fundamental. Membranes vibrate in two dimensions, producing inharmonic overtones (first overtone ~1.59× fundamental, not 2×), giving a center pitch rather than a clean harmonic note.

column1: Why can timpani be tuned to a specific orchestral pitch while toms cannot?
column2: The timpani's parabolic kettle couples air mass to the membrane, pulling the first several vibrational modes into near-harmonic alignment — unlike toms, whose inharmonic modes only produce a general 'pitched noise' center tone.

column1: What determines whether a drum's 'crack' sounds crisp/dry versus buzzy/sensitive?
column2: Snare wire tension against the resonant (bottom) head: tight tension gives a crisp, dry crack but less sensitivity to quiet strokes; loose tension gives a buzzy, more sensitive sound (good for ghost notes) but can rattle unintentionally.

column1: In the verbal subdivision counting system ('1 e & a, 2 e & a...'), why is being able to count a rhythm out loud at tempo considered a prerequisite for playing it accurately?
column2: The voice functions as a rhythm debugger — if you can't verbally articulate each 16th-note subdivision slot in time, you don't yet have the internal rhythmic grid needed to place strokes accurately; sight-reading failures are almost always rhythm failures, not symbol failures.
